name: Routing Across Automated Market Makers
title: Routing Across Automated Market Makers
answer: Routing across automated market makers is the practice of splitting and directing a trade across multiple on-chain liquidity pools to improve execution relative to a single pool. It covers token swaps, stablecoin exchanges, and larger orders where price impact and slippage matter. The scope includes choosing venues, splitting order size, setting limits, and handling failed or partial fills. It sits in crypto markets and decentralised finance, where AMMs replace order books with pooled liquidity and algorithmic pricing.

sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Routers run on blockchain nodes and RPC endpoints, smart contracts, and indexers that read pool states. They depend on mempool data, block builders, and gas price feeds. Aggregator contracts hold allowances and execute multi-hop swaps atomically. Off-chain services compute routes and submit transactions, while on-chain contracts enforce the swap.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: A router models each pool's pricing curve, fees, and available liquidity, then searches over paths, splits, and hop counts. Optimization can be exact for small graphs or heuristic and learning-based for larger ones. Simulation against recent blocks estimates output and gas. Slippage tolerance and deadline parameters bound execution. MEV considerations like sandwich attacks and backrunning shape how transactions are sent.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Risks include smart contract bugs, oracle or price manipulation, MEV extraction, failed transactions, and liquidity changes between quote and execution. Provenance matters for route data, pool addresses, and contract versions. Regulatory treatment of DeFi routing varies by jurisdiction, and compliance pages track that. The site's 215 compliance and regulation pages are a reference point for policy changes.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Routing is moving toward intent-based systems, solver auctions, and cross-chain swaps. AI methods may improve path search and slippage prediction. Account abstraction and private mempools could change how routes are submitted. Competition among aggregators and AMM designs will keep execution quality and transparency central.
